script.opening: "Something’s not right, doctor. I’m hungry all the time — I can’t stop eating — yet I’ve actually lost weight. I’m constantly thirsty, I’m up several times a night to wee, and I’m shattered. It’s come on over a few weeks. What’s going on?"

facts.text: About 6 weeks. Always hungry, eating more than usual, yet clothes are looser — belt two notches tighter. Very thirsty — drinking "loads", mostly full-sugar fizzy drinks. Up 3–4 times a night to pass urine. Exhausted. Blurred vision when reading lately.

If asked: "The nurse did a finger-prick — she said my sugar was 21 and my ketones were 0.4, and there was sugar in my urine but no ketones. She weighed me: 96 kilos — I was 102 in the spring." Blood pressure 138/86.
No vomiting, no tummy pain, not drowsy or confused, not breathless. Eating and drinking fine.
No palpitations, tremor or heat intolerance. No cough, night sweats or lumps. No infections, no thrush or balanitis. No tingling in the feet. No diarrhoea.
Overweight for years. "Nothing regular." No allergies. Mother has type 2 diabetes; his sister has "an underactive thyroid". Smokes 10 a day, drinks about 15 units a week.
Delivery driver for a supermarket — drives a car-sized van (no HGV licence). Married, two teenage children. Wife is worried about his weight loss.
Worried but practical. You wondered about diabetes, but the weight loss scared you: "So it’s not cancer?" Ask "Will I be able to keep driving?" Admit the fizzy drinks when thirst is discussed.

ice.ideas: "I wondered about diabetes, with my mum having it."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "The weight loss scared me. I thought it could be something worse" (cancer). Also worried about his driving job.

cues: "I’ve lost weight" — needs both diabetes type assessment and his cancer fear addressed.
"I drive for a living" — DVLA and safe driving advice.
"I’ve been drinking loads of fizzy drinks" — worsens hyperglycaemia; simple advice.

checkpoints.text: Recognises POLYPHAGIA with the OSMOTIC symptoms (polydipsia, polyuria, weight loss, fatigue) as likely new DIABETES, considering type 2 vs type 1/LADA (NICE NG17: not excluded on age or BMI alone)

Screens for and EXCLUDES DKA/acute decompensation (vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, Kussmaul breathing, ketotic breath, dehydration) — a same-day EMERGENCY — checking capillary glucose AND ketones

CONFIRMS the diagnosis appropriately (capillary glucose and ketones now; laboratory fasting/random plasma glucose per WHO criteria), recognising HbA1c is not appropriate with symptoms under two months or suspected type 1
Differentiates other causes of polyphagia + weight loss where atypical (hyperthyroidism — TFTs, malignancy, malabsorption)

Initiates TYPE 2 management (lifestyle, NICE NG28 February 2026 dual first-line modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor, introduced stepwise, cardiovascular risk per NICE NG238, education, complication screening — eyes/feet/renal, DVLA advice) OR refers urgently/admits if DKA or type 1 is suspected
Explains the likely diagnosis and plan clearly, addresses his concern, and checks understanding
Checks how the symptoms and the prospect of diabetes are affecting him, motivates engagement with lifestyle change without lecturing, and agrees clear next steps together

Safety-nets and follows up: same-day/urgent assessment if DKA/type-1 features, diagnostic confirmation and management initiation, complication screening, and review — recognising diabetes and excluding DKA, not delay

worked.txt: "Those symptoms together — constant hunger and thirst, weeing a lot, losing weight despite eating, and exhaustion — strongly suggest your blood sugar is high; in other words, diabetes. Let me check it right now with a finger-prick."

"A few important checks — any vomiting, tummy pain, drowsiness, or fast deep breathing? … No, and you’re not dehydrated. I’ll also check for ketones, because if your sugar is very high with ketones you can become seriously unwell and need same-day hospital care."

"Your glucose is high. I’ll confirm with a laboratory glucose test — the usual HbA1c test can under-read when symptoms have only been there a few weeks — and given your symptoms that’s usually enough to diagnose diabetes. The pattern fits type 2, but because you’re under 50 and losing weight I’ll keep the type that needs insulin in mind."
"If anything didn’t fit, I’d also check your thyroid and look for other causes of weight loss — but the thirst and weeing point clearly to diabetes here."

"For type 2, we start with diet and lifestyle and usually two tablets that work as a pair: a slow-release tablet called metformin first, then a second called an SGLT2 inhibitor added within a few weeks, look after your heart risk, arrange eye, foot and kidney checks, and get you proper diabetes education. With those tablets you don’t need to tell the DVLA for a normal car licence. We’ll do this step by step."
"If you become very unwell — vomiting, drowsy, breathing fast, severe tummy pain — that’s an emergency, call 999 or go straight to A&E. Otherwise we’ll get your tests done and start treatment."

f.learning: POLYPHAGIA (increased appetite/constant hunger) with the OSMOTIC symptoms of hyperglycaemia — POLYDIPSIA (thirst), POLYURIA (excess urination), unexplained WEIGHT LOSS despite eating, and fatigue — is the classic cluster of new DIABETES, commonly TYPE 2 in an overweight, middle-aged patient with family history, though TYPE 1/LADA must be considered — NICE NG17 features are ketosis, rapid weight loss, age under 50, BMI below 25 and autoimmune history, and age or BMI alone must not exclude it. Critically, screen for and exclude acute decompensation/DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS — being very unwell, vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness/confusion, deep rapid (Kussmaul) breathing, ketotic ("pear-drop") breath and dehydration — which is a medical emergency needing same-day assessment/admission (especially if type 1 is suspected), so check capillary glucose AND ketones. Confirm the diagnosis appropriately (capillary glucose and ketones now; laboratory fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 / random ≥11.1 with symptoms; HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol only where appropriate), noting that in a symptomatic patient one diagnostic test suffices and that WHO 2011 (international) advises against HbA1c for diagnosis when symptoms are under two months or type 1 is suspected (use plasma glucose). Where the picture is atypical or glucose normal, differentiate other causes of polyphagia with weight loss — hyperthyroidism (TFTs), malignancy, malabsorption — but the osmotic symptoms strongly point to diabetes. For confirmed type 2 diabetes, initiate management per NICE NG28 (lifestyle, modified-release metformin then an SGLT2 inhibitor with DKA counselling, renal considerations, structured education), cardiovascular-risk management (NICE NG238 atorvastatin 20 mg if QRISK 10% or more), complication screening — retinal, foot, renal/ACR — and DVLA advice, and refer urgently/admit if DKA or type 1 is suspected. Safety-net for deterioration. NICE NG12: new-onset diabetes with weight loss at 60 or over prompts urgent pancreatic imaging — not applicable at 48, but reassess weight loss that continues after glucose control.

knowledge.guideline: [1] WHO diagnostic criteria for diabetes (2006) and use of HbA1c in diagnosis (2011) (international) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes in adults: management (updated February 2026) · [3] NICE NG17 Type 1 diabetes in adults: diagnosis and management · [4] Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care: management of DKA in adults (revised March 2023) · [5] NICE NG238 Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification (2023) · [7] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: diabetes mellitus · [8] MHRA Drug Safety Update: SGLT2 inhibitors and diabetic ketoacidosis (March 2020)
knowledge.summary: Polyphagia with thirst, polyuria and weight loss over weeks is hyperglycaemia until proved otherwise. The first job is to decide whether he is safe to stay in the community: a capillary glucose and ketone check, and a screen for vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, rapid breathing and dehydration. Then confirm diabetes with a laboratory plasma glucose, because HbA1c can under-read when symptoms have been present for under two months [1]. Although type 2 is likeliest in an overweight man with a family history, weight loss and age under 50 are features that NG17 [3] asks you to weigh for type 1. If type 2 is confirmed, NG28 (February 2026) [2] recommends modified-release metformin first, then adding an SGLT2 inhibitor, alongside education, cardiovascular risk reduction and complication screening.

points.t: WHO [1]: with classic symptoms, one abnormal result confirms diabetes: random plasma glucose 11.1 mmol/L or more, fasting plasma glucose 7.0 mmol/L or more, or HbA1c 48 mmol/mol or more. HbA1c is not appropriate for diagnosis when symptoms have been present for less than two months, when type 1 is suspected, in acute illness, in pregnancy, or in conditions affecting red cell turnover [1]; use plasma glucose. A capillary meter reading is a triage tool, not a diagnostic test.

NG17 [3]: diagnose type 1 clinically in adults with hyperglycaemia and one or more of: ketosis, rapid weight loss, age under 50, BMI below 25, or a personal or family history of autoimmune disease; do not use age or BMI alone to exclude it. Marcus is 48 with weight loss, so type 1 or latent autoimmune diabetes must be actively considered even though he is overweight. If ketones are raised or type 1 is suspected, discuss with the diabetes or acute medical team the same day.

JBDS [4] defines DKA as ketones 3.0 mmol/L or more (or significant ketonuria), glucose above 11 mmol/L or known diabetes, and bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and/or venous pH below 7.3. Warning features: vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, deep rapid breathing, ketotic breath, dehydration. Marked hyperglycaemia with dehydration and confusion without ketosis suggests a hyperosmolar state. Either needs emergency admission.

NG28 (February 2026) [2]: offer structured education and lifestyle support; for most adults needing medication, offer dual first-line therapy: modified-release metformin (in preference to standard release unless swallowing needs dictate, titrated to the tolerated dose) plus an SGLT2 inhibitor, introduced stepwise with the SGLT2 inhibitor added within weeks, unless contraindicated and with caution in frailty. Before an SGLT2 inhibitor, check DKA risk factors and counsel on ketoacidosis and sick-day rules [8]. Doses per BNF. Typical HbA1c target 48 mmol/mol on lifestyle or drugs without hypoglycaemia risk, individualised.

Check BP, lipids and QRISK: NG238 [5] recommends offering atorvastatin 20 mg when 10-year risk is 10% or more. Arrange retinal screening, foot assessment, urine ACR and eGFR, and weight support. NICE NG12 [6]: new-onset diabetes with weight loss at 60 or over prompts urgent pancreatic imaging; at 48 this criterion does not apply, but weight loss that continues after glucose control needs reassessment.

If glucose is normal, think of hyperthyroidism (TFTs), malabsorption and malignancy. DVLA [7]: Group 1 drivers treated with diet, metformin or an SGLT2 inhibitor alone do not need to notify; insulin or sulfonylureas bring hypoglycaemia rules, and different rules apply to Group 2 licences.

model.text: Hello Mr Hale, I’m Dr Evans. What’s brought you in today?

Something’s not right, doctor. I’m hungry all the time, I can’t stop eating, yet I’ve lost weight. I’m constantly thirsty, I’m up several times a night to wee, and I’m shattered. It’s come on over a few weeks. What’s going on?
That sounds exhausting, and worrying when the weight is dropping despite eating. I’d like to ask a few quick questions and check your sugar with a finger-prick straight away, if that’s all right.
model.why: Recognises the osmotic cluster; immediate capillary glucose

model.text: Go ahead.
Have you been sick at all, had tummy pain, felt drowsy or muddled, or noticed you’re breathing faster or deeper than usual?
No, none of that. Just tired and thirsty.
Are you managing to keep fluids down, and how much weight do you think you’ve lost?
model.why: Dehydration and rate of weight loss

model.text: Drinking loads. My clothes are looser, but I haven’t weighed myself.
Any blurred vision, infections like thrush, slow-healing cuts, or tingling in your feet?
No, I don’t think so.
And to rule out other causes of hunger with weight loss: any shakiness, heat intolerance, palpitations, diarrhoea, or blood in your stools?
No. Nothing like that.
Who in the family has diabetes, and do you know which type? Any family history of thyroid or other autoimmune conditions?
model.why: Family history relevant to type 1 versus 2

model.text: I know there’s diabetes in the family. I’m not sure of the details.
Do you take any medicines, including steroids? And do you drive, and if so, for work?
Nothing regular. I drive a car, that’s all.
Your finger-prick sugar is high, well above normal. I’m also checking your blood ketones, which tell me whether your body is starting to break down fat because it can’t use sugar properly.
model.why: Capillary ketones: the key safety test

model.text: Your ketones are normal and your pulse, blood pressure and breathing are fine, and you don’t look dry. That means you’re safe to be managed from here today.
model.why: Documents the decision not to admit, with reasons

model.text: Before I explain, what had you been thinking this might be?
I wondered about diabetes, with the family. But the weight loss scared me. I thought it could be something worse.

I’m glad you said that. I think this is diabetes: when sugar is high, it spills into the urine, taking water with it, so you’re thirsty, and your body can’t use the sugar, so you feel hungry and lose weight. That explains everything you’ve described, including the weight loss.
model.why: Explains the mechanism and answers the cancer worry

model.text: So it’s not cancer?

The pattern fits diabetes very well. If the weight keeps falling once your sugar is under control, I’ll look further. I need to confirm with a laboratory glucose test, because the usual HbA1c test can under-read when symptoms have only been there a few weeks.
model.why: Plasma glucose rather than HbA1c for short-duration symptoms

model.text: Most people your age and build have type 2. But because you’re under 50 and losing weight, I need to keep type 1 in mind, which needs insulin. If your ketones rise or you get worse quickly, that changes the plan the same day.
Today: a lab glucose, HbA1c as a baseline, kidney function, cholesterol, thyroid, liver tests and a urine test for protein. I’ll see you again within the week with the results.

If it’s type 2, the usual start is a slow-release metformin tablet, increased gradually, and then a second tablet called an SGLT2 inhibitor added within a few weeks — the two together are now the usual first treatment — along with a course on living with diabetes. We’ll arrange eye screening, foot and kidney checks, and look at your heart risk.
model.why: NG28 February 2026 initial treatment and care processes

model.text: Will I be able to keep driving?
Yes. With those tablets you don’t need to tell the DVLA for a normal car licence. That would change if you ever needed insulin.
How do you feel about changes to what you eat and drink? What would be realistic for you?
I could cut the fizzy drinks. I’ve been drinking loads because of the thirst.
That’s a great start: switch to water now, because sugary drinks will push your sugar higher.
If you start vomiting, get tummy pain, feel drowsy or breathless, or can’t keep fluids down, that’s an emergency: call 999 or go to A&E. Can you tell me the plan in your own words?
Blood tests today, water not fizzy drinks, back in a week, and A&E if I’m sick or drowsy.
Exactly. We’ll take this step by step together.

social.t: Sugary drinks taken for thirst worsen hyperglycaemia. Work patterns and shift work shape meal timing and medication choices.
First-degree relatives share the risk; offering them risk assessment is reasonable.

legal.t: Group 1 drivers on diet, metformin or SGLT2 inhibitors alone need not notify. Insulin or sulfonylureas bring hypoglycaemia-awareness rules; Group 2 licences have stricter rules.
People with diabetes treated with medication are entitled to a medical exemption certificate in England.

professional.t: Record the ketone result and the reasoning for community management; arrange timely review of confirmatory results.
Discuss benefits and side effects of metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors, including genital infection and DKA risk, and record the conversation.

community.t: Structured education programme (e.g. DESMOND), NHS Diabetes Prevention and weight services where eligible, diabetic eye screening, Diabetes UK.

redFlags: Vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, deep rapid breathing, ketotic breath: suspected DKA, emergency
Confusion with marked dehydration: suspected hyperosmolar state, emergency
Raised capillary ketones or rapid progression: same-day diabetes or medical team
Weight loss with new diabetes at 60 or over: NICE NG12 pancreatic imaging (not met at 48)
psychosocial: Fear that weight loss means cancer
Diet, sugary drinks and family patterns
ice: Concern: the weight loss means something worse
Expectation: an explanation and a plan

playbook.diagnosis: “Your symptoms and the high sugar reading point to diabetes, most likely type 2. I’ll confirm it with a lab test today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Insulin is the key that lets sugar into your cells. If the key isn’t working, sugar builds up in the blood and spills into the urine, taking water with it, while your cells go hungry. That’s why you’re thirsty, weeing more, hungry and losing weight.”

management.reflectIce: “You were frightened the weight loss meant cancer. The pattern fits diabetes very well, and I’ll keep checking your weight as things settle.”
management.psychosocial: Build on his own chosen change; address driving; offer education rather than a lecture.
sharedPlan: Lab plasma glucose; HbA1c baseline, U&E, lipids, TFT, LFT, urine ACR
If type 2: NG28 (Feb 2026) dual first-line — MR metformin, with an SGLT2 inhibitor added within weeks; doses per BNF
Structured education; switch sugary drinks to water
QRISK and statin per NG238; retinal, foot and kidney checks
Same-day diabetes team if ketones rise or type 1 suspected
safetyNet: Vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, breathlessness: 999 or A&E
Review within a week with results; reassess if weight keeps falling

pitfalls.intro: The station checks whether you recognise a new diabetic who may be decompensating, confirm the diagnosis correctly, and avoid anchoring on type 2.

items.fail: No capillary glucose or ketone check at the visit.
items.why: Ketones decide whether he can safely go home.
items.fix: Check glucose and ketones and record the decision.

items.fail: Relying on HbA1c alone to diagnose after a few weeks of symptoms.
items.why: WHO 2011: HbA1c is not appropriate when symptoms are under two months; it can under-read.

items.fail: Assuming type 2 because he is overweight.
items.why: NG17: age under 50 and weight loss are type 1 features; BMI alone does not exclude it.
items.fix: Keep type 1 in mind and act the same day if ketones rise.

items.fail: Starting standard-release metformin alone as the whole plan.
items.why: NG28 (Feb 2026) makes modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor dual first-line for most adults, plus education and risk reduction.
items.fix: Follow the updated sequence with care processes.

items.fail: Ignoring the fear that weight loss means cancer.
items.why: It is his main concern and affects how he hears the plan.
items.fix: Address it directly and say what would prompt more tests.

items.why: DKA can develop quickly if this is type 1.
items.fix: Name vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness and breathlessness as 999 features.

timeMap.d: Let him list the symptoms; offer a finger-prick glucose now.
Vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, breathing, fluids; other hyperglycaemic symptoms; thyroid and bowel; family history; medicines; driving.
Capillary glucose and ketones; obs; hydration. Decide community versus same-day.
ICE; mechanism; plasma glucose not HbA1c alone; type 1 kept in mind; bloods; NG28 treatment path; DVLA; one lifestyle change.
Emergency features; review within a week; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Books a routine HbA1c and sends him home without checking glucose or ketones; misses DKA features; starts treatment without confirming the diagnosis; ignores the cancer worry.
wordPics.pass: Checks capillary glucose and ketones, screens for DKA, confirms diabetes with appropriate tests, starts type 2 management and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: knows HbA1c can under-read with symptoms under two months, weighs NG17 type 1 features in a 48-year-old losing weight, uses the NG28 (Feb 2026) sequence, gives DVLA advice, and answers the cancer fear directly.

avoid.dont: “Let’s do an HbA1c and I’ll see you in a couple of weeks.”
avoid.instead: “The nurse checked your sugar and ketones this morning; I’ll confirm with a lab glucose.”
avoid.why: A delay can miss DKA, and HbA1c can under-read after only weeks of symptoms.

avoid.dont: “You’re overweight, so it’s bound to be type 2.”
avoid.instead: “Type 2 is most likely, but your weight loss means I’ll keep type 1 in mind.”
avoid.why: NG17 advises against using BMI or age alone to exclude type 1.

avoid.dont: “You need to lose weight and stop eating so much.”
avoid.instead: “Your hunger is caused by the high sugar. What change feels realistic to start with?”
avoid.why: Blame undermines engagement; polyphagia is a symptom, not a failing.

Blood tests today, water not fizzy drinks, back in a week, and A&E if I’m sick or drowsy.
Exactly. We’ll take this step by step together.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] WHO diagnostic criteria for diabetes (2006) and use of HbA1c in diagnosis (2011) (international) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes in adults: management (updated February 2026) · [3] NICE NG17 Type 1 diabetes in adults: diagnosis and management · [4] Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care: management of DKA in adults (revised March 2023) · [5] NICE NG238 Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification (2023) · [7] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: diabetes mellitus · [8] MHRA Drug Safety Update: SGLT2 inhibitors and diabetic ketoacidosis (March 2020)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Polyphagia with thirst, polyuria and weight loss over weeks is hyperglycaemia until proved otherwise. The first job is to decide whether he is safe to stay in the community: a capillary glucose and ketone check, and a screen for vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, rapid breathing and dehydration. Then confirm diabetes with a laboratory plasma glucose, because HbA1c can under-read when symptoms have been present for under two months [1]. Although type 2 is likeliest in an overweight man with a family history, weight loss and age under 50 are features that NG17 [3] asks you to weigh for type 1. If type 2 is confirmed, NG28 (February 2026) [2] recommends modified-release metformin first, then adding an SGLT2 inhibitor, alongside education, cardiovascular risk reduction and complication screening.

points.t: WHO [1]: with classic symptoms, one abnormal result confirms diabetes: random plasma glucose 11.1 mmol/L or more, fasting plasma glucose 7.0 mmol/L or more, or HbA1c 48 mmol/mol or more. HbA1c is not appropriate for diagnosis when symptoms have been present for less than two months, when type 1 is suspected, in acute illness, in pregnancy, or in conditions affecting red cell turnover [1]; use plasma glucose. A capillary meter reading is a triage tool, not a diagnostic test.

NG17 [3]: diagnose type 1 clinically in adults with hyperglycaemia and one or more of: ketosis, rapid weight loss, age under 50, BMI below 25, or a personal or family history of autoimmune disease; do not use age or BMI alone to exclude it. Marcus is 48 with weight loss, so type 1 or latent autoimmune diabetes must be actively considered even though he is overweight. If ketones are raised or type 1 is suspected, discuss with the diabetes or acute medical team the same day.

JBDS [4] defines DKA as ketones 3.0 mmol/L or more (or significant ketonuria), glucose above 11 mmol/L or known diabetes, and bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and/or venous pH below 7.3. Warning features: vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, deep rapid breathing, ketotic breath, dehydration. Marked hyperglycaemia with dehydration and confusion without ketosis suggests a hyperosmolar state. Either needs emergency admission.

NG28 (February 2026) [2]: offer structured education and lifestyle support; for most adults needing medication, offer dual first-line therapy: modified-release metformin (in preference to standard release unless swallowing needs dictate, titrated to the tolerated dose) plus an SGLT2 inhibitor, introduced stepwise with the SGLT2 inhibitor added within weeks, unless contraindicated and with caution in frailty. Before an SGLT2 inhibitor, check DKA risk factors and counsel on ketoacidosis and sick-day rules [8]. Doses per BNF. Typical HbA1c target 48 mmol/mol on lifestyle or drugs without hypoglycaemia risk, individualised.

Check BP, lipids and QRISK: NG238 [5] recommends offering atorvastatin 20 mg when 10-year risk is 10% or more. Arrange retinal screening, foot assessment, urine ACR and eGFR, and weight support. NICE NG12 [6]: new-onset diabetes with weight loss at 60 or over prompts urgent pancreatic imaging; at 48 this criterion does not apply, but weight loss that continues after glucose control needs reassessment.

If glucose is normal, think of hyperthyroidism (TFTs), malabsorption and malignancy. DVLA [7]: Group 1 drivers treated with diet, metformin or an SGLT2 inhibitor alone do not need to notify; insulin or sulfonylureas bring hypoglycaemia rules, and different rules apply to Group 2 licences.

social.t: Sugary drinks taken for thirst worsen hyperglycaemia. Work patterns and shift work shape meal timing and medication choices.
First-degree relatives share the risk; offering them risk assessment is reasonable.

legal.t: Group 1 drivers on diet, metformin or SGLT2 inhibitors alone need not notify. Insulin or sulfonylureas bring hypoglycaemia-awareness rules; Group 2 licences have stricter rules.
People with diabetes treated with medication are entitled to a medical exemption certificate in England.

professional.t: Record the ketone result and the reasoning for community management; arrange timely review of confirmatory results.
Discuss benefits and side effects of metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors, including genital infection and DKA risk, and record the conversation.

community.t: Structured education programme (e.g. DESMOND), NHS Diabetes Prevention and weight services where eligible, diabetic eye screening, Diabetes UK.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Your symptoms and the high sugar reading point to diabetes, most likely type 2. I’ll confirm it with a lab test today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Insulin is the key that lets sugar into your cells. If the key isn’t working, sugar builds up in the blood and spills into the urine, taking water with it, while your cells go hungry. That’s why you’re thirsty, weeing more, hungry and losing weight.”

management.reflectIce: “You were frightened the weight loss meant cancer. The pattern fits diabetes very well, and I’ll keep checking your weight as things settle.”
management.psychosocial: Build on his own chosen change; address driving; offer education rather than a lecture.

Same-day diabetes team if ketones rise or type 1 suspected

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The station checks whether you recognise a new diabetic who may be decompensating, confirm the diagnosis correctly, and avoid anchoring on type 2.

items.fail: No capillary glucose or ketone check at the visit.
items.why: Ketones decide whether he can safely go home.
items.fix: Check glucose and ketones and record the decision.

items.fail: Relying on HbA1c alone to diagnose after a few weeks of symptoms.
items.why: WHO 2011: HbA1c is not appropriate when symptoms are under two months; it can under-read.

items.fail: Assuming type 2 because he is overweight.
items.why: NG17: age under 50 and weight loss are type 1 features; BMI alone does not exclude it.
items.fix: Keep type 1 in mind and act the same day if ketones rise.

items.fail: Starting standard-release metformin alone as the whole plan.
items.why: NG28 (Feb 2026) makes modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor dual first-line for most adults, plus education and risk reduction.
items.fix: Follow the updated sequence with care processes.

items.fail: Ignoring the fear that weight loss means cancer.
items.why: It is his main concern and affects how he hears the plan.
items.fix: Address it directly and say what would prompt more tests.

items.why: DKA can develop quickly if this is type 1.
items.fix: Name vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness and breathlessness as 999 features.
